cues.text: A Pope's Unexpected Announcement
Elected in 1958 at age seventy-six, John XXIII was widely expected to be a brief, transitional pope.

Less than three months into his pontificate, he startled the Church by announcing his intention to convoke a new ecumenical council—the first since Vatican I had been interrupted, unfinished, in 1870.

John spoke of a program of aggiornamento , an Italian word meaning "updating" or "bringing up to date," seeking not to change Catholic doctrine but to present it in language and forms suited to the modern world.
After more than three years of preparatory work by commissions across the Church, the council opened at St. Peter's Basilica on October 11, 1962 .
John XXIII delivered his address, Gaudet Mater Ecclesiae , explicitly rejecting what he called the "prophets of doom".
They saw only decline and crisis facing the Church, while he called instead for a confident, pastoral renewal.
An Unprecedented Assembly
Vatican II drew between 2,000 and 2,500 bishops, patriarchs, and cardinals from every part of the world.
They attended each of its four autumn sessions between 1962 and 1965, making it by far the largest and most geographically representative council in the Church's history.
It reflected the global spread of Catholicism far beyond its historic European heartlands.

For the first time, official observers from Protestant and Orthodox communities were invited to attend, alongside a small number of lay auditors, including women, participating for the first time in the deliberations of an ecumenical council.
John XXIII died in June 1963, midway through the council's work; his successor, Paul VI , resumed and completed the sessions, guiding the council to its close on December 8, 1965 .
Sixteen Documents

Over its four sessions, the council produced sixteen documents of varying authority: four major constitutions — on the sacred liturgy ( Sacrosanctum Concilium ), the nature of the Church ( Lumen Gentium ), and divine revelation ( Dei Verbum ).

They also addressed the Church's relationship to the modern world ( Gaudium et Spes ), along with nine decrees and three declarations covering topics from bishops and priests to religious life, ecumenism, non-Christian religions, and religious freedom.

Sacrosanctum Concilium initiated the most visible change most Catholics experienced: a wide-ranging reform of the liturgy that permitted, among other things, greater use of vernacular languages in place of Latin and increased lay participation in the Mass.
Ecumenism and Religious Freedom
Vatican II marked a significant shift in the Catholic Church's posture toward other Christians and other religions.
Unitatis Redintegratio committed the Church to active ecumenical dialogue with Orthodox and Protestant Christians.
It described them as separated brethren rather than simply outside the Church's bounds.

Nostra Aetate addressed the Church's relationship to non-Christian religions, notably repudiating collective Jewish responsibility for Christ's death and condemning antisemitism in unusually direct terms for a conciliar document.
Dignitatis Humanae , among the council's most debated documents, affirmed a right to religious freedom rooted in the dignity of the human person.
This position required careful theological reconciliation with earlier magisterial statements more cautious about the civil toleration of religious error.
Legacy
The Second Vatican Council stands as the most consequential event in modern Catholic history.

It reshaped the Church's liturgy, self-understanding, and relationship with the wider world so significantly that Catholic life is still commonly described as either "pre-conciliar" or "post-conciliar."
Its reception has itself been a subject of vigorous ongoing debate within the Church, over how its documents should be interpreted and how faithfully its reforms have been implemented.
That debate continued actively through the pontificates of John Paul II, Benedict XVI, and Francis, and remains a live conversation in Catholic theology to the present day.
